Why Compare These Two?

If you're a DIYer, homeowner, mechanic, or plumbing enthusiast, you've probably needed to peek inside a wall, check behind an engine block, or see what's clogging a drain. That's where an inspection borescope becomes indispensable.

Both of these cameras are standalone — meaning they have their own built-in screen, so you don't need to tether them to your phone or tablet. That's a massive advantage over cheap WiFi endoscopes that drop connections at the worst possible moment.

We put them head-to-head on build quality, display clarity, cable flexibility, included accessories, and overall bang for your buck.

🔍 Detailed Breakdown

Display Quality

Both cameras feature a 4.3-inch IPS color screen — large enough to see detail clearly without squinting. The Inspection Borescope offers a 170° horizontal viewing angle and lets you switch between three observation modes with a single button. That's particularly handy when you're working in tight spaces and can't reposition the camera easily.

The DEPSTECH also has split-screen capability, showing the front and side views simultaneously, which is genuinely useful for navigating pipes and cavities. Both are crisp and bright enough to use in direct sunlight with adjustable backlighting.

Edge: Near tie, but the Inspection Borescope's three-mode button switching is more intuitive on the fly.

Camera & Probe Design

The Inspection Borescope uses a 7.9mm probe head — slightly slimmer than the DEPSTECH's 8.0mm. That 0.1mm difference matters when you're trying to thread the camera through a narrow pipe bend or a tight engine compartment. Both use semi-rigid cabling that holds its shape — meaning you can bend the cable and it stays put, unlike cheap fully-flexible endoscopes that flop around.

Both are IP67 waterproof, so you can submerge them in drains, coolant reservoirs, or fish tanks without worry. The 8-LED ring on the Inspection Borescope is one more LED than the DEPSTECH's 7, giving marginally better illumination in dark spaces.

Edge: Inspection Borescope — slimmer probe, brighter LEDs.

Recording & Sharing

The DEPSTECH pulls ahead here by including a 32GB microSD card in the box. You can snap photos and record 1080P video directly to the card, then pop it into your computer for review. The Inspection Borescope can also record but uses a Type-C data cable connection to transfer files — it doesn't include a memory card in the package.

For most DIY jobs, snapping quick reference photos matters more than video. If you need ongoing documentation (e.g., for insurance claims or contractor disputes), the included SD card is a nice convenience.

Edge: DEPSTECH — 32GB card included saves you a separate purchase.

Accessories

Both kits include the essential borescope accessories: a hook (for grabbing loose debris), a magnet (for retrieving metal objects), and a side mirror (for looking around corners).

The Inspection Borescope comes with a Type-C data cable and a more ergonomic handle design. Users consistently mention that the handle feels natural for extended use — important when you're spending 30+ minutes inspecting ductwork or engine bays.

Edge: Inspection Borescope — better ergonomics, Type-C connectivity.

Ease of Use

This is where both cameras shine over phone-based endoscopes. No WiFi pairing. No app downloads. No Bluetooth handshakes. You turn the unit on, point the camera, and start inspecting. That's the right approach for a tool you'll grab when something is already broken and you're frustrated.

The Inspection Borescope has a slight edge in simplicity with a single-button mode toggle and an instinctively placed brightness control. The DEPSTECH's button layout is fine but slightly busier with the photo/video recording controls.

Edge: Inspection Borescope — simpler controls, less fumbling.

❓ Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a phone or tablet to use these borescopes?

No! Both have a built-in 4.3-inch IPS screen. They are completely standalone. This is actually their biggest advantage over cheap WiFi endoscopes that need a phone and often drop connection.

Can I use these in wet environments?

Yes — both are rated IP67 waterproof. The camera probe can be submerged in water without damage. Great for checking drains, pipes, fish tanks, or coolant systems.

How long is the cable?

Both feature a 16.5-foot (5-meter) semi-rigid cable. It's long enough for most automotive and home inspection tasks. The semi-rigid design means you can bend it to hold its shape, unlike fully flexible cables that won't stay where you point them.

Can the cable go around corners?

The camera is semi-rigid, not steerable. You can pre-bend the cable to roughly the shape you need, then push it into the cavity. For navigating sharp 90° bends in plumbing, the side mirror attachment helps you see around corners.

Which is better for automotive work?

Both work well for checking cylinder walls, looking behind engine blocks, and inspecting wiring harnesses. The Inspection Borescope's 7.9mm slimmer probe and brighter 8-LED ring give it a slight edge for tight engine bay spaces.
